SAT1001.name: Abuse existing OAuth integrations
SAT1001.summary_first: Some SaaS apps allow OAuth integrations to other apps, which allow the app to gain access to certain data and additional functionality.

SAT1002.name: Account ambushing
SAT1002.summary_first: Many SaaS apps have features that can be used to effectively backdoor an account, such as the ability to configure multiple login methods or create API keys to access the account programmatically.

SAT1003.name: Account recovery
SAT1003.summary_first: Most SaaS apps allow accounts to be recovered via email.

SAT1004.name: API keys
SAT1004.summary_first: Many SaaS apps let you configure an API key to enable programmatic access.

SAT1005.name: API secret theft
SAT1005.summary_first: Apps that support integrations through API keys (rather than the more common OAuth integrations) will sometimes allow those keys to be read after being set.

SAT1006.name: App directory lookup
SAT1006.summary_first: SaaS apps will generally have a user directory and often this is visible to any user of the app.

SAT1007.name: App spraying
SAT1007.summary_first: An adversary may attempt to authenticate to a SaaS account by guessing a large number of passwords.

SAT1008.name: Automation workflow sharing
SAT1008.summary_first: Some SaaS automation apps allow pre-configured automations to be shared with other users.

SAT1009.name: Client-side app spoofing
SAT1009.summary_first: Some OAuth integrations intended for use by desktop or mobile clients (rather than typical SaaS-to-SaaS integrations) can be controlled by adversaries.

references.title: Maintaining persistent access in a SaaS-first world

SAT1010.name: Consent phishing
SAT1010.summary_first: OAuth allows users to grant third-party apps permissions to access their data.

references.title: Decoding consent phishing - technical blog post
O365 attack toolkit - perform consent phishing attacks against O365
Compromised Microsoft Partner Network accounts used for consent phishing

SAT1011.name: Credential stuffing
SAT1011.summary_first: Credential stuffing is the re-use of stolen credentials, often from leaked password databases, in an attempt to authenticate to other apps.

SAT1012.name: Device code phishing
SAT1012.summary_first: OAuth supports multiple different authentication flows that can be used to grant access to an app.

references.title: Introducing a new phishing technique for compromising Office 365 accounts
How to Detect Malicious OAuth Device Code Phishing
PhishInSuits - a tool for device code phishing vs SMS
Microsoft device code documentation

SAT1013.name: DNS reconnaissance
SAT1013.summary_first: Some SaaS apps require ownership verification for a domain as part of the setup process.

SAT1014.name: Email discovery
SAT1014.summary_first: There is generally evidence in a user’s mailbox when they are actively using a SaaS app.

SAT1015.name: Email phishing
SAT1015.summary_first: Email phishing is the classic social engineering attack that involves an email being sent to a target user with an embedded link or malicious attachment.

references.title: Evilginx - MITM framework for phishing login credentials

SAT1016.name: Evil twin integrations
SAT1016.summary_first: OAuth apps provide a mechanism for maintaining long-term persistent access to compromised accounts that resist normal recovery actions, such as password resets.

references.title: Maintaining persistent access in a SaaS-first world - Technical blog post
The shadow workflow's evil twin - Technical blog post

SAT1017.name: Ghost logins
SAT1017.summary_first: A common SaaS app feature allows logins to the same account using multiple methods simultaneously – for example, a standard password-based authentication (local to the SaaS app) and an SSO mechanism, such as an OIDC social login or SAML login.

references.title: X thread explaining ghost logins with reference to Snowflake
Google email verification flaw abused to compromise 3rd party SaaS services

SAT1018.name: IM phishing
SAT1018.summary_first: Traditionally, phishing attacks have been mostly email-based.

references.title: Slack Attack: A phisher's guide to initial access
Slack Attack: A phisher's guide to persistence and lateral movement
Jumpsec Advisory: IDOR in Microsoft Teams Allows for External Tenants to Introduce Malware
TeamsPhisher
Slack Jack - A tool for Slack bot token abuse
Evilginx - AITM framework for phishing login credentials
Storm-0324 distributes malware using TeamsPhisher

SAT1019.name: IM user spoofing
SAT1019.summary_first: Some instant messaging apps do not strongly control the way a user presents themselves in terms of display names, full names, user handles, photos, and so on.

references.title: Slack Attack: A phisher's guide to initial access
Slack Attack: A phisher's guide to persistence and lateral movement

SAT1020.name: In-app phishing
SAT1020.summary_first: It’s possible to conduct phishing and other social engineering attacks, using native features of SaaS apps.

references.title: Jade sleet compromise using GitHub repository collaboration
Evilginx - MITM framework for phishing login credentials
Phishing lures embedded within shared documents
GitHub notification phishing

SAT1021.name: Link backdooring
SAT1021.summary_first: Users have long been trained to be wary of clicking links from external sources such as email.

references.title: Evilginx - MITM framework for phishing login credentials

SAT1022.name: Link sharing
SAT1022.summary_first: Many SaaS apps offer the ability to share items with third parties through sharing links.

SAT1023.name: Malicious mail rules
SAT1023.summary_first: Common SaaS mail providers like Office365 and Gmail provide mail rule functionality that allows users to automate certain tasks on their mailboxes.

references.title: Malicious Outlook Rules - Technical blog post
Ruler - A tool to abuse Exchange services
XRulez - A command line tool for creating malicious outlook rules
Multi-account Office365 compromise using mail rules
Microsoft blog - Mail rules used to hide attacks

SAT1024.name: MFA fatigue
SAT1024.summary_first: One of the most common implementations of MFA is using push notifications to a mobile device that allow the user to approve or deny the login request.

references.title: Uber breach by Lapsus$

SAT1025.name: nOAuth
SAT1025.summary_first: SaaS apps that make use of OAuth integrations require an identifier to match accounts between the application and identity provider.

references.title: nOAuth: How Microsoft OAuth Misconfiguration Can Lead to Full Account Takeover

SAT1026.name: OAuth token enumeration
SAT1026.summary_first: SaaS app users may have authenticated using OIDC (social logins) or have created other OAuth integrations to share data and make better use of the app.

SAT1027.name: OAuth tokens
SAT1027.summary_first: An adversary can use a malicious OAuth app or API development tool to create an OAuth token, using arbitrary permissions to maintain long-term programmatic access to a compromised user account.

references.title: Microsoft blog - Threat actors misuse OAuth applications to automate financially driven attacks
Microsoft blog - Midnight Blizzard using OAuth for persistence in attack against MS

SAT1028.name: Password scraping
SAT1028.summary_first: While it may not be security good practice, many teams stored passwords in cleartext, especially shared or system credentials.

references.title: Abusing Okta SWA - Technical blog post
Can my admins steal my cloud password manager secrets? - Technical blog post

SAT1029.name: Passwordless logins
SAT1029.summary_first: Some SaaS apps allow passwordless email-based authentication, where an OTP is sent via email when a login is requested, rather than a user having a standard password.

SAT1030.name: Poisoned tenants
SAT1030.summary_first: An adversary can register a new tenant that it controls and administers with the intent of tricking users to join it, by convincing them it is owned by their organization.

references.title: SAMLjacking a poisoned tenant - Technical blog post

SAT1031.name: SAML enumeration
SAT1031.summary_first: It’s often possible to determine if an organization is using a SaaS app by checking whether a SAML login IdP has been configured for the organization domain.

SAT1032.name: SAMLjacking
SAT1032.summary_first: When configuring SAML integrations for a SaaS app, you must provide a URL to an IdP service so the app can hand-off authentication during the SAML flow.

references.title: Evilginx - MITM framework for phishing login credentials
SAMLjacking a poisoned tenant - Technical blog post

SAT1033.name: Shadow workflows
SAT1033.summary_first: The SaaS world is, by design, largely abstracted away from operating systems and application binaries.

references.title: Living off the Cloud. Cloudy with a Chance of Exfiltration
The shadow workflow's evil twin - Technical blog post
Slack Attack: A phisher's guide to persistence and lateral movement
Octo Tempest use FiveTran to steal SalesForce and ZenDesk databases

SAT1034.name: Slug tenant enumeration
SAT1034.summary_first: SaaS vendors make use of different strategies to separate tenants from one another.

SAT1035.name: Subdomain tenant discovery
SAT1035.summary_first: SaaS vendors make use of different strategies to separate different tenants from one another.

SAT1036.name: System integrations
SAT1036.summary_first: Some SaaS apps allow OAuth integrations that are not tied to a user account, but to the app tenant, or a machine account instead.

references.title: Slack Attack: A phisher's guide to persistence and lateral movement
Slack Jack - A tool for Slack bot token abuse

SAT1037.name: Takeout services
SAT1037.summary_first: Takeout services allow users to export all of their data from a SaaS app into a downloadable format.

SAT1038.name: Username enumeration
SAT1038.summary_first: When attempting to authenticate to a SaaS app, the login mechanism itself may disclose whether the username/email address is a known/valid account, even if the provided password is incorrect.

references.title: Holehe - OSINT tool for finding registered accounts

SAT1039.name: Webhooks
SAT1039.summary_first: Some SaaS apps allow webhooks to be configured so callbacks are made when certain events are triggered.

SAT1040.name: Hijack OAuth flows
SAT1040.summary_first: During the OAuth authorization code flow, after a user grants permission to a third-party application, the service provider generates an authorization code and redirects the user's browser back to the third-party application's specified *redirect_uri*.
examples: HackerOne - OAuth redirect_uri bypass using IDN homograph attack resulting in user's access token leakage
HackerOne - Stealing Users OAuth authorization code via redirect_uri

references.title: OWASP - Testing for OAuth Authorization Server Weaknesses
PortSwigger - OAuth 2.0 authentication vulnerabilities
PortSwigger - Hidden OAuth attack vectors

SAT1041.name: Inbound federation
SAT1041.summary_first: Inbound federation allows users to login to a target identity provider by authenticating with a source identity provider.

references.title: Okta Cross-Tenant Impersonation

SAT1042.name: AiTM Phishing
SAT1042.summary_first: Attacker-in-the-Middle (AITM) phishing is a newer variant of phishing that uses dedicated tooling to act as a web proxy between the victim and a legitimate login portal for an application the victim has access to, principally to make it easier to defeat MFA protection.

references.title: Evilginx - AITM web proxy
EvilnoVNC - AITM noVNC proxy
Modlishka- AITM web proxy
Muraena - AITM web proxy
NoPhish - AITM noVNC proxy

SAT1043.name: Device Enrollment
SAT1043.summary_first: Some attack techniques result in temporary access to an account being obtained, possibly including knowledge of the account password, such as through AiTM phishing that proxies MFA codes or similar.

references.title: NCSC advisory on cloud attacks by APT29
Scattered Spider Attack Analysis - Technical Blog
APT29 Attack Analysis - Technical Blog

SAT1044.name: Session cookie theft
SAT1044.summary_first: Due to increasing use of SaaS apps, core identity providers acting as SSO gateways to them, and the widespread adoption of MFA, hybrid attacks involving the theft of valid browser session cookies from compromised endpoints using infostealing malware are becoming more common.

references.title: 2024 Sophos Threat Report
Traffers - a deep dive into the information stealer ecosystem

SAT1045.name: MFA downgrade
SAT1045.summary_first: Phishing-resistant MFA factors, such as passkeys or vendor-specific implementations like Okta Fastpass, have been introduced to deal with the problem of [AiTM phishing attacks](/techniques/aitm_phishing/description.md) and credential theft.
examples: Microsoft - Windows Hello for Business MFA downgrade attack

references.title: FIDO Alliance - Passkeys 101
X33fcon - Unraveling and Countering Adversary-in-the-Middle Phishing Attacks - MFA downgrade section
Evilginx phishlet for WHfB MFA downgrade attack

SAT1046.name: Guest Access Abuse
SAT1046.summary_first: In SaaS platforms like Salesforce, ServiceNow, and Zendesk, misconfigurations related to guest user permissions can lead to unauthorized data access or escalation of privileges.
examples: Salesforce guest user misconfiguration allowing data access
ServiceNow instance where guest users could access PII Data

references.title: Give Secure Access to Unauthenticated Users with the Guest User Profile
General Information | Potential Public List Widget Misconfiguration

SAT1047.name: Cross-IdP Impersonation
SAT1047.summary_first: Cross-IdP impersonation is when an adversary uses an account with the correct target email address but registered with an identity provider that is not in use by the target organization to authenticate to a target SaaS application.

references.title: Technical blog post - Verification phishing and cross-idp impersonation
Zendesk vulnerability allows Slack compromise

SAT1048.name: Verification phishing
SAT1048.summary_first: Email verification is sometimes used as a control, such as when registering new accounts.

references.title: Technical blog post - Verification phishing and cross-idp impersonation

SAT1049.name: UI redressing
SAT1049.summary_first: UI redressing attacks can be used to trick a user into performing an action on a legitimate application that is different to what they perceived.

references.title: OWASP - Clickjacking
Technical blog - DoubleClickjacking: A New Era of UI Redressing

SAT1050.name: App-specific password phishing
SAT1050.summary_first: App-Specific password phishing is a social engineering technique where an adversary tricks a user into generating an "app-specific password" for their account and then sharing it with the attacker.

references.title: Technical blog - Russian Government-Linked Social Engineering Targets App-Specific Passwords

SAT1051.name: ConsentFix
SAT1051.summary_first: ConsentFix is a social engineering technique that combines ClickFix-style deception with OAuth authorization code theft.

references.title: ConsentFix - Push Security blog
